1.2.d: Two or more independent clauses joined by coordination (and, but, or) or punctuation.
1.2.e: "It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen." (George Orwell, 1984)

1.3.d: One independent clause and at least one dependent (subordinate) clause.
1.3.e: "The boy stood on the burning deck, whence all but him had fled." (Felicia Hemans, Casabianca)

1.4.d: At least two independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses.
1.4.e: "He was an old man who fished alone in a skiff in the Gulf Stream and he had gone eighty-four days now without taking a fish." (Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea)

1.5.d: Independent clauses joined by semicolons, colons, or dashes without coordinating conjunctions.
1.5.e: "To be, or not to be: that is the question." (William Shakespeare, Hamlet)

1.7d.d: Makes a statement or expresses an opinion.
1.7d.e: "Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation…" (Abraham Lincoln, Gettysburg Address)

1.7i.e: "What light through yonder window breaks?" (William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet)

1.7m.d: Gives a command, request, or instruction (see also 5.7.6).
1.7m.e: "Do not go gentle into that good night." (Dylan Thomas)

1.7e.d: Expresses strong emotion, surprise, or emphasis.
1.7e.e: "What a piece of work is a man!" (William Shakespeare, Hamlet)

1.7t.d: A declarative sentence with a short interrogative tag appended, reversing the polarity of the main clause.

2.1.d: Able to stand alone as a complete sentence.

2.2.d: Cannot stand alone; attaches to an independent clause, often introduced by a subordinating conjunction (because, although, when, if).
2.2.e: "as long as it stays inside the maze." (Margaret Atwood, The Handmaid's Tale)

2.3.d: A dependent clause functioning as a noun — subject, object, or complement; often introduced by that, what, whoever. An expletive it can delay it to the end.
2.3.e: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." (Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice)

2.4.d: A dependent clause functioning as an adverb — time, place, reason, condition, concession, manner, or purpose.
2.4.e: "If music be the food of love, play on." (William Shakespeare, Twelfth Night)

2.5.d: A dependent clause functioning as an adjective, modifying a noun or pronoun; introduced by a relative pronoun (who, whom, whose, which, that) or relative adverb.
2.5.e: "the Grinch, who lived just north of Who-ville, did NOT!" (Dr. Seuss)

2.6.d: Functional roles within a clause: subject, verb, direct object, indirect object, subject complement, object complement, adverbial.
2.6.e: "I shot the sheriff." (Bob Marley — "the sheriff" is the direct object)

3.1.d: A group of words centred on a noun (determiners, adjectives, etc.).

3.2.d: A group of words centred on a verb, including auxiliaries.

3.3.d: Preposition + its object (usually a noun phrase).
3.3.e: "From there to here, from here to there, funny things are everywhere." (Dr. Seuss)

3.4.d: Group of words that modifies a noun.

3.5.d: Group of words modifying a verb, adjective, or another adverb.

3.6.d: Headed by a participle (-ing or -ed/-en), functioning as an adjective.
3.6.e: "…the child sleeping beside him." (Cormac McCarthy, The Road)

3.7.d: Headed by "to" + base verb; functions as noun, adjective, or adverb.
3.7.e: "To be, or not to be: that is the question." (Shakespeare, Hamlet)

3.8.d: Headed by a gerund (-ing verb form) functioning as a noun.

3.9.d: Modifies an entire clause; noun + modifier without a finite verb, carrying its own internal subject — overlapping with the verbless clause (2.8).
3.9.e: "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past." (F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby)

3.10.d: A noun phrase that renames or explains an adjacent noun; essential (no commas) or non-essential (commas).
3.10.e: "Atticus Finch, a quiet and dignified lawyer in Maycomb, defended an innocent man." (Harper Lee)

4.1n.d: Names a person, place, thing, or idea (common, proper, countable, uncountable, collective, abstract).

4.1v.d: Expresses an action, state, or occurrence (main, auxiliary, modal; transitive, intransitive; finite, non-finite).

4.1adv.d: Modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb.

4.1pron.d: Replaces a noun (personal, possessive, reflexive, relative, demonstrative, indefinite, interrogative, reciprocal).
4.1pron.e: "What light through yonder window breaks?" (Shakespeare — interrogative)

4.1prep.d: Shows a relationship between a noun/pronoun and other words.

4.1conj.d: Joins words, phrases, or clauses (coordinating, subordinating, correlative).

4.1det.d: Introduces and specifies a noun (a, an, the, this, some…).

4.3.1.d: Base form (3rd-person singular adds -s/-es): habits, facts, scheduled future, timeless truths.
4.3.1.e: “All happy families are alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.” (Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina)

4.3.2.d: am/is/are + -ing: actions happening now, temporary situations, changing/developing situations.

4.3.3.d: have/has + past participle: actions with present relevance, life experience, unfinished time periods.

4.3.4.d: have/has been + -ing: actions that started in the past and continue, or have recently stopped with visible results.
4.3.4.e: “I have been working on this for years.”

4.3.5.d: -ed or irregular form: completed actions at a specific past time, sequences of events.
4.3.5.e: “It was a bright cold day in April.” (George Orwell, 1984)

4.3.6.d: was/were + -ing: ongoing actions in the past, background actions, interrupted actions.

4.3.7.d: had + past participle: an action completed before another past action (backshifting).
4.3.7.e: “She had gone eighty-four days now without taking a fish.” (Hemingway)

4.3.8.d: had been + -ing: ongoing action before another past point.
4.3.8.e: “She had been waiting three hours before the letter came.”

4.3.9.d: will + base (or be going to): predictions, spontaneous decisions, planned future.
4.3.9.e: “I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree.” (W.B. Yeats, The Lake Isle of Innisfree)

4.3.10.d: will be + -ing: in progress at a future time.
4.3.10.e: “This time tomorrow I will be flying over the Atlantic.”

4.3.11.d: will have + past participle: completed before a future point.
4.3.11.e: “By the time you read this, I will have left.” (common epistolary style)

4.3.12.d: will have been + -ing: duration up to a future point.
4.3.12.e: “By June I will have been teaching for twenty years.”

4.4.1.d: Indefinite a/an for non-specific singular countables; definite the for known nouns; zero article for general plurals/uncountables.

4.4.2.e: "This above all: to thine own self be true." (Hamlet)

4.4.3.d: my, your, his, her, its, our, their — ownership or relationship.

4.4.4.d: Expresses amount or number: much/many/a lot of; little/few; all/some/any/no; each/every.
4.4.4.e: "A person's a person, no matter how small." (Dr. Seuss)

4.4.5.d: Cardinal and ordinal numbers are classified as quantifiers/determiners, not adjectives: they precede true adjectives, cannot be graded, and cannot be predicative.
4.4.5.e: "Four score and seven years ago…" (Lincoln) / "…eighty-four days…" (Hemingway)

4.5.d: A small word (up, off, out…) forming a phrasal verb whose meaning is not the sum of its parts; particles can move past a noun object and must follow a pronoun object.
4.5.e: "Never gonna give you up, never gonna let you down." (Rick Astley)

5.1.1.d: Subject and verb must agree in number and person. English shows three concord types: grammatical (agreement with the subject’s form), notional (agreement with its meaning — standard in British English for collective nouns), and proximity/attraction (agreement with the nearest noun — legitimate with either…or, but an error when it overrides a clear head; see 7.3).

5.1.2.d: Pronouns agree with their antecedents in number, gender, and person.

5.2.1.d: Opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose.
5.2.1.e: "a lovely small old round red Italian leather handbag"

5.3.1.d: Elements in a list, comparison, or coordinated structure must share grammatical form.
5.3.1.e: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times…" (Dickens)

5.3.2.d: The subject may be omitted when clear from context — common in imperatives and compounds.

5.3.3.d: The subordinator "that" may be omitted before a nominal dependent clause.
5.3.3.e: "Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again." (du Maurier, Rebecca)

5.3.4.d: "There" as dummy subject asserting existence; the notional subject follows the verb and controls agreement.
5.3.4.e: "There was no possibility of taking a walk that day." (Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre)

5.5.1.d: Subject receives the action: be + past participle (+ by-agent).
5.5.1.e: "The cat was chased by the dog."

5.5.2.d: Modal verbs express necessity, possibility, permission, or ability (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would); they are auxiliaries (4.8), followed by the bare infinitive. Two readings — epistemic (how likely the speaker judges something) and deontic (obligation/permission) — are not points on one scale. Semi-modals (have to, ought to, need to, be able to, used to) supply the forms true modals lack.

5.6.1.d: not, n't, never, no reverse meaning; negating a main verb requires do-support.
5.6.1.e: "I do not like green eggs and ham." (Dr. Seuss)

5.6.2.d: Two negatives make a non-standard positive in standard English.

5.7.1.d: Special verb forms for hypothetical, wished, or suggested situations.
5.7.1.e: "…as if she were the sun…" (Tolstoy, Anna Karenina)

5.7.2.d: Splits information for emphasis with "it is/was" or "what".
5.7.2.e: "It was the dog that barked loudly."

5.7.5.d: Reversed subject–verb order for questions, emphasis, or after negative adverbs.
5.7.5.e: "Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset."

5.7.6.d: Commands and requests with implied "you"; may take flat adverbs.
5.7.6.e: "Do not go gentle into that good night." (Dylan Thomas)

5.7.7.d: Direct speech quotes exact words; indirect speech embeds them with backshifted tense and shifted pronouns.
5.7.7.e: "Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn." → Rhett said that he didn't give a damn.

5.8.1.d: Deliberate repetition of coordinating conjunctions for rhythm or magnitude.
5.8.1.e: "Think left and think right and think low and think high." (Dr. Seuss)

6.4.d: Capitals mark sentence starts, proper nouns, the pronoun "I", and titles.
6.4.e: "Toto, I've a feeling we're not in Kansas anymore." (The Wizard of Oz)

7.4.d: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma (splice) or nothing (fused). Fix with a period, a semicolon, or a comma + coordinating conjunction.
7.4.e: "It was raining heavily, we decided to stay inside." (incorrect)

7.5.d: A phrase or dependent clause punctuated as a full sentence — missing a subject, finite verb, or complete thought.
7.5.e: "Because the dog barked loudly all night." (incorrect)

7.6.d: A list or compound mixing grammatical forms (e.g. gerunds with infinitives). See rule 5.3.1.
7.6.e: "She enjoys reading, swimming, and to ride her bike." (incorrect)

7.9.d: Wrong subjective/objective case, especially in compounds or after prepositions.
7.9.e: "The secret is between you and I." → "…between you and me."

7.10.d: its/it's, your/you're, their/they're/there — the apostrophe form is always the contraction. Test by expanding it.

7.11.d: more/most combined with an already-inflected form; one degree marker only.
7.11.e: "the most unkindest cut of all" (Julius Caesar — deliberate)

1.6.n: Sentences with mixed coordination and subordination
1.6.d: Combines coordination, subordination, and punctuation for more elaborate structures.
1.6.e: “I meant what I said and I said what I meant.” (Dr. Seuss, Horton Hatches the Egg)

2.7.d: A clause whose verb is non-finite (no tense or subject agreement), usually with the subject unexpressed — to-infinitival, bare infinitival, gerund-participial, or past-participial. The same material catalogued at phrase level in 3.6–3.8.

2.8.d: A clause with a subject and a predicative element but no verb at all. Compare 3.9 (Absolute Phrase), with which this overlaps.

2.9.d: A dependent clause making a comparison, introduced by “than” or the “as…as” frame, or by the correlative “the…the” construction.
2.9.e: “The more you practise, the better you become.”

2.10.d: A short clause inserted into or appended to another to mark the speaker’s stance, without normal subordination marking.

3.11.d: Two or more phrases of the same type joined by a coordinating conjunction, together filling a single slot — the phrasal counterpart of clause coordination (1.2).

3.12.d: Phrases nest recursively inside larger phrases — the recursion that lets a finite grammar generate unbounded sentences.
3.12.e: “She ran quickly through the dark forest” — an adverb phrase and a prepositional phrase whose object is itself a noun phrase.

4.2.d: Inflection (plurals, tenses, degrees of comparison) varies a word’s form within its class; derivation (prefixes, suffixes, compounding) makes a new word, often in a new class. Other processes: conversion, clipping, blending, back-formation, acronymy.
4.2.e: “happy → unhappy → unhappiness” (derivation) vs “walk / walks / walked” (inflection, still a verb)

4.6.d: Every English verb has at most five forms — base, 3rd-person singular -s, past, past participle, present participle — from which all tense/aspect combinations are built; “be” is the sole exception, with eight. Finite forms carry tense and subject agreement; non-finite forms do not (see 2.7).
4.6.e: “She runs every morning, though she is tired of running.” (finite “runs”; non-finite gerund “running”)

4.7.d: Verbs differ in how many arguments they require: intransitive, transitive, ditransitive, complex-transitive, copular/linking. See the clause patterns catalogued in 2.6.

4.8.n: Auxiliary vs main verb — the NICE properties
4.8.d: Auxiliaries are distinguished from main verbs by four behaviours: Negation directly, Inversion in questions, Code (standing in for an elided predicate), and Emphasis (carrying stress). Main verbs need do-support (5.6.1).
4.8.e: “She can swim and so can he.” (Code)

4.9.d: Dynamic verbs denote actions and take the progressive; stative verbs denote states and normally resist it (know, own, believe, seem). Some verbs shift between the two with a change of sense.
4.9.e: “I think it’s true” (stative) vs “I’m thinking about it” (dynamic)

4.10.d: Gradable words admit degree and comparison (tall → taller → tallest; beautiful → more beautiful); non-gradable words (dead, unique, pregnant) resist both degree modifiers and comparison. See 7.11.

4.11.d: English pronouns inflect for case: subjective (I, he, she, we, they), objective (me, him, her, us, them), and possessive (my/mine, his, her/hers, our/ours, their/theirs). Case is determined by the pronoun’s function, not its position. See 7.9.
4.11.e: “He and I went” (subjective) vs “between you and me” (objective)

4.12.d: The infinitive combines with auxiliaries to form six forms — bare, to-infinitive, perfect, progressive, perfect progressive, passive — marking aspect and voice while remaining non-finite throughout (see 4.6).

5.1.3.d: They/them/their used of a single person whose gender is unknown, unspecified, or non-binary. Now standard in formal English and recognised by the major dictionaries. It takes plural verb forms regardless.
5.1.3.e: “Each student should bring their own copy.”

5.2.2.d: Conventional sequence of adverbials: manner → place → frequency → time → purpose.
5.2.2.e: “She sang beautifully in the hall every evening last week for charity.”

5.4.1.d: Maintain logical tense progression within a sentence or paragraph unless a deliberate shift is signalled.

5.4.2.d: Correct choice and placement of articles (a, an, the) and quantifiers.
5.4.2.e: “She saw an elephant at the zoo.” (not “a elephant”)

5.7.3.d: Non-restrictive (extra information, commas) vs restrictive (essential, no commas). American usage reserves “that” for restrictive clauses and “which” for non-restrictive; British usage permits “which” in both, relying on the commas — not the pronoun — as the reliable signal.
5.7.3.e: “The books that are on the table are mine.” (restrictive) vs “The books, which are on the table, are mine.” (non-restrictive)

5.7.4.d: Four standard types: zero (general truth), first (real future possibility), second (hypothetical present/future), third (counterfactual past); plus mixed conditionals and inverted forms that drop “if”.
5.7.4.e: “If I were you, I would resign.” (second conditional)

5.9.d: English prefers given information early and new information late (end-focus), and heavy constituents late (end-weight) — the motive behind the passive (5.5.1), clefts (5.7.2), extraposition/dummy subjects (2.3, 5.3.4), and fronting.
5.9.e: “It surprised everyone that he had lied all along.” (extraposed, vs “That he had lied all along surprised everyone.”)

6.1.d: Periods, question marks, exclamation marks, semicolons, colons, em/en dashes, quotation marks, hyphens, parentheses, and ellipses each clarify meaning and structure in a distinct way.
6.1.e: “To be, or not to be: that is the question.” (colon introducing an explanation)

6.2.d: Commas separate items in lists, set off introductory phrases and non-restrictive clauses (5.7.3), precede coordinating conjunctions in compound sentences, and mark direct address. The serial (Oxford) comma resolves genuine ambiguity in lists of three or more.

6.3.d: Marks possession (singular adds ’s; plural ending in s adds ’) and omitted letters in contractions. Possessive pronouns (its, yours, theirs, ours, hers, his) take no apostrophe.

6.5.d: The two traditions differ in quotation-mark nesting (British: single outer, double inner; American: the reverse) and in whether commas/full stops fall inside or outside the closing quotation mark (American: always inside; British: inside only when part of the quoted matter). This catalogue follows British convention throughout.

7.1.d: A modifier whose implied subject never actually appears in the sentence, so it attaches, illogically, to whatever subject the main clause does supply — distinct from a misplaced modifier (7.2) and a squinting modifier (7.12).
7.1.e: “Running late, the bus left without me.” (incorrect) → “Running late, I found the bus had already left.”

7.2.d: A modifier positioned too far from the word it is meant to describe, so it appears to modify something else instead.
7.2.e: “She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates.” (incorrect) → “She served the children sandwiches on paper plates.”

7.3.n: Agreement errors with collective nouns or indefinite pronouns
7.3.d: Giving a collective noun or indefinite pronoun the wrong concord for the sense intended (see 5.1.1 for grammatical vs notional concord).
7.3.e: “The team are winning.” (British notional concord) vs “The team is winning.” (American grammatical concord)

7.7.d: A pronoun that could refer to more than one antecedent, or that refers to a vague, generalised idea rather than a specific noun.
7.7.e: “When the car hit the tree, it was badly damaged.” (incorrect — was the car or the tree damaged?)

7.8.d: Starting a sentence with one grammatical structure and shifting halfway through to an incompatible one, leaving the sentence syntactically broken.
7.8.e: “By studying every night is how she passed the exam.” (incorrect) → “By studying every night, she passed the exam.”

7.12.d: A modifier positioned so it could attach to what precedes it or what follows, leaving the sentence genuinely ambiguous — distinct from dangling (7.1, no referent) and misplaced (7.2, wrong referent).
7.12.e: “Students who revise essays regularly improve their writing.” → “Students who regularly revise essays improve their writing.” (forcing one reading)

7.13.d: A subject and predicate that cannot logically combine, even when the syntax is well-formed. Common triggers: “is when”, “is where”, “the reason … is because”.
7.13.e: “Arachnophobia is when someone fears spiders.” (incorrect) → “Arachnophobia is the fear of spiders.”

7.14.d: An unmotivated change of grammatical person or number within a sentence or paragraph.
7.14.e: “I enjoy hiking because you can see nature up close.” (incorrect) → “I enjoy hiking because I can see nature up close.”
